title: Microphone: Sound Into Numbers
description: Component lesson. Sound is just air pushing back and forth. A microphone's whole job is turning that push into a number, over and over, very fast.

content.value: Every sensor in this course does the same fundamental job: turn something physical into a number. A microphone's version of that job is turning air pressure changes — sound — into an electrical signal, and eventually into numbers a controller can read.

Inside is a thin membrane, free to vibrate. Sound waves are nothing more than air pressure pushing and pulling rapidly — when they reach the membrane, it physically vibrates along with them. That vibration is converted into a changing electrical voltage, which a controller can sample thousands of times a second and record as a sequence of numbers: a waveform.

content.title: 🎙️ See the waveform
content.hint: Switch to Microphone mode — notice how irregular and unpredictable a real sound's waveform looks, nothing like a clean tone.

content.value: A pure musical note looks like a clean, regular sine wave — smooth and repeating. Real sound, like a voice, looks messy and irregular, layering many frequencies and volumes on top of each other at once. That messiness is genuinely useful: it's what makes voices distinguishable from each other at all.

That waveform is only step one of "hearing" in the way Module 11 will mean it. Turning a waveform into actual words is a much bigger job — you'll meet that pipeline properly when this course gets to AI.
Key takeaway: a microphone's membrane vibrates with incoming sound pressure, and that vibration becomes an electrical signal a controller can sample as a waveform — a sequence of numbers over time.

quiz.question: What physically vibrates inside a microphone when sound arrives?
options: A thin membrane, moved by the air pressure changes of the sound wave
quiz.explain: Sound is pressure pushing and pulling on the membrane, and that motion is what gets converted to an electrical signal.

quiz.question: Why does a real voice's waveform look so much messier than a single musical tone's?
options: A voice layers many frequencies and volumes together at once, unlike a single clean tone
quiz.explain: That irregular, layered complexity is genuinely part of the signal — it's what makes each voice sound distinct.

quiz.question: What does a microphone's waveform give you that's not yet the same as understanding what was said?
options: A raw sequence of numbers over time — turning that into words is a separate, later step
quiz.explain: The waveform is the raw material. Converting it into recognised words is a much bigger job, covered later in the AI module.
